topic.title: The photographer runs the wedding
topic.claim: At Indian weddings now, the rituals wait for the photographer, because the album is the part the relatives will actually see.
topic.moment: The pandit pauses the pheras while the camera team asks the couple to 'do that again, slowly'.

turn.actually: They're about the footage, because the reel reaches more people than the venue holds.

topic.because: The reel gets shown for years and travels further than the event. So the timeline is built around light and angles.

topic.behaviour: Couples book the photo team first and plan rituals around golden hour and drone shots.
topic.mechanism: Footage reaches more people than the event.

mechanism.broken_premise: None. Most of the post is cultural reading and opinion: the photographer 'outranking' the pandit, rituals fitting around light, couples barely remembering the day. Those are interpretations, not claims I can check. The factual claims it relies on are plausible and match vendor sources. The photographer is often one of the first vendors booked, popular dates go 9–18 months ahead, and multi-day coverage is commonly priced from about ₹1 lakh to ₹10–15 lakh in metros. I found no source showing it is false that photographers are 'sometimes booked before the venue.' Two caveats. First, 'a quote in lakhs' fits mid-to-premium teams, while solo photographers can charge ₹30,000–60,000. Second, venues can limit crews and equipment, so the photographer's schedule doesn't always win.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Wedding photo and video teams price by team size, number of event days (haldi, mehendi, sangeet, wedding, reception), drones and album or film deliverables. That's why multi-day coverage often costs lakhs. Good teams fill peak muhurat dates 9–18 months ahead, which pushes couples to lock them in early, sometimes before other vendors. How much the shoot shapes the day is down to each family and the planner. The pandit's muhurat and the venue's rules still set the outer limits.

cover.headline: Indian weddings run on the [photographer's clock]
cover.sub: The album outlives the mandap, and every planner knows it.

paragraphs: Indian weddings run on the photographer's clock, because the album outlives the mandap.
slides.why_swipe: What does that actually look like on the day?

paragraphs: The couple's grand entry. Halfway down, the camera team asks them to "do that again, slowly." So they walk back and do it again, same smile.
Two hundred guests watch the retake with their plates in hand. Nobody even blinks.
slides.why_swipe: Is it just that one moment, or the whole wedding?

paragraphs: The wedding guides spell it out. At least an hour for couple portraits. Thirty minutes per group shot. Drones at golden hour, and the family warned where not to stand.
slides.why_swipe: Why would families let the camera outrank the ritual?

paragraphs: Think about who the day is really for. The wedding happens once, for whoever fits in the hall.
The film plays for years. On the family WhatsApp group, on every cousin's phone, every time someone asks to see it. So the day gets built around light and angles, and the rituals fit in between.
It's not even vanity. For every relative who couldn't make it, the reel is the wedding.
Only problem? The couple barely remembers the day. They were too busy hitting their marks.
slides.why_swipe: So who is really running the wedding?

paragraphs: At the next wedding, watch who says "ek baar aur, please."

That's the person in charge.
It's never the pandit.

end.save: Open it again when the photographer sends you the wedding-day timeline.
end.send: Send to the friend getting married in December, who already has the photographer's timeline open.

draft.alt_text: A seven-slide text post arguing that Indian weddings run on the photographer's schedule. During the couple's grand entry, the camera team asks them to do it again, slowly, and two hundred guests watch the retake as if it's normal. It points out that wedding guides advise keeping at least an hour for couple portraits, thirty minutes per group shot, drone shots at golden hour, and warning the family where not to stand. It argues that the wedding happens once for whoever fits in the hall, while the film plays for years on family phones, so the day is planned around light and angles. It says this isn't even vanity, because for relatives who couldn't make it, the reel is the wedding, though the couple barely remembers the day. It ends by saying that whoever says 'one more time' is the person in charge, and it's never the pandit.

claims.text: Wedding guides advise allocating at least an hour for couple portraits and 30 minutes per group shot in the wedding-day timeline.
Wedding drone shots are advised to be scheduled at golden hour, with guests and family informed beforehand to prevent obstructions.
